title: Tenant pod-level reservation API and discrete burst arbitration
creator: Lena Park
description: Summary: This PRD defines a tenant-facing API and backend semantics for allocating 'pod-level' soft reservations (atomic GPU/slot units) and an arbitration mechanism that permits discrete bursts with deterministic preemption hints. Motivation: We need a lightweight, predictable reservation primitive for Dedicated customers who need near-guaranteed capacity for short bursts while preserving cluster fairness and minimizing tail latency. Current reserved pools are coarse-grained and either overcommit or require heavy operator intervention. The pod-level reservation concept lets tenants request small atomic units (1..N pods) with time-bounded soft guarantees and explicit fallback behavior when contention occurs. This PRD covers API surface, orchestration semantics, failure/fallback policies, observability, and acceptance criteria.
background: Redwood's Dedicated offering currently exposes reserved pools and headroom controls. Customers with bursty workloads (search, chat-heavy product pages, realtime inference pipelines) ask for small, short-lived guarantees without buying large reserved capacity. Engineering has experimented with micro-reserves, but the behaviour has been opaque: opaque preemption rules, inconsistent telemetry, and poor integration with autoscaling. This causes customer confusion and operational overhead.
goals: Expose a simple REST/SDK API for tenants to create, query, and release pod-level soft reservations
Ensure deterministic arbitration: when capacity is scarce, decide fallback/preemption using tenant priority, age, and fairness windows
Integrate with autoscaler so pods can be prewarmed based on active soft reservations
Provide observability: per-reservation metrics, traces on fallbacks/preemptions, and cost accounting
Keep tail latency SLOs for non-reserved traffic within 1.5x baseline under burst conditions
non_goals: This PRD is not introducing hard preemptible instances with billing changes
Not changing existing Reserved Pool contract semantics (billing/commit tiers remain intact)
Not replacing tenant-level long-lived reservations (those remain for large committed capacity)
Not designing an external marketplace for trading reservation credits
user_stories: As an engineering lead I want to request a 10-second soft reservation of 2 pods before a product demo so that latency remains stable for the demo period
As an SRE I want clear telemetry showing which reservations were preempted during an incident to debug noisy tenants
As a platform engineer I want autoscaler to prewarm nodes when there are pending soft reservations to avoid cold-start latency
As a product PM I want tenants to be able to set fallback policies (use cheaper model variant / queue / failover region) per reservation
requirements: API: POST /v1/dedicated/reservations - accept tenant_id, num_pods, duration_seconds, priority_tier, fallback_policy, optional tag
API: GET /v1/dedicated/reservations/{id} - returns state (PENDING | ACTIVE | PREEMPTED | EXPIRED | FAILED), allocated_pods, and telemetry links
API: PATCH /v1/dedicated/reservations/{id} - allow extend duration up to a configurable cap and allow voluntary release
Semantic: Reservations are soft guarantees. ACTIVE means system has pinned capacity for the reservation window; PREEMPTED means pinned capacity was reclaimed earlier due to higher-priority demand
Arbitration: Deterministic comparator: (priority_tier desc, reservation_age asc, tenant_decay_score asc) to choose who keeps pod(s) under contention
Preemption hooks: Platform should call tenant-configured URL webhook and emit an event into tenant audit stream 5s before forced preemption when possible
Autoscaler integration: pending reservations increment a soft headroom target so the autoscaler attempts prewarm up to a configurable limit
Billing/Accounting: tag reservations to attribute cost and emit reservation-level token usage metrics; no change to base billing model in first iteration
Quota enforcement: Respect tenant entitlement; reservations above entitlement return 409 with recommended fallback
Observability: emit metrics (reservation.created, reservation.activated, reservation.preempted, reservation.fallback_applied) and a reservation trace id that ties to request replay logs
Graceful fallback: Platform must support per-reservation fallback policies: queue (with TTL), fallback_model_variant, region_fallback, or reject
Safety: Cap maximum concurrent soft reserved pods per zone and global to avoid high contention on small clusters
constraints: Kubernetes node warm-up time is non-deterministic; autoscaler improvements are required to meet short reservation windows
Control plane must avoid synchronous blocking operations on reservation creation under heavy load
We cannot change existing tenant SLAs for Dedicated customers in this release
Cross-zone reservations will be advisory only in v1 (no cross-zone atomic allocation guarantee)
acceptance_criteria: API contract implemented and documented in Redwood API spec with SDK examples
E2E test that creates 50 concurrent short reservations and verifies at least 95% of ACTIVE reservations either succeed or apply configured graceful fallback within SLA
Arbitration deterministic: simulation harness reproducibly ranks reservations using comparator and test vectors
Autoscaler prewarm: when 80% of reservations are PENDING, autoscaler increases target capacity to meet 70% of requested pods within configured warm-up time in staging
Preemption webhook: when forced preemption occurs, webhook call and audit event recorded for all preempted reservations in 95% of cases
Observability: dashboards show reservation success rate, preemption rate, average reservation lead time, and cost attribution per tenant
Safety caps enforced and returned errors for requests exceeding caps documented and surfaced with clear remediation guidance
Canary rollout: feature enabled for a single pilot tenant and internal test accounts for 2 weeks with monitoring alerts before broad rollout
success_metrics: Reservation activation rate >= 90% for pilot tenants under typical load
Median tail latency for non-reserved traffic under burst <= 1.3x baseline
Reduction in customer support tickets related to short-term capacity by 40% for pilot tenants
Autoscaler prewarm accuracy: >=70% of reserved pods healthy and ready within warm-up window
rollout_plan: Phase 1: Implement API + backend orchestration + basic autoscaler hooks in staging. Pilot with two existing Dedicated customers and internal perf test tenants (2 weeks). Phase 2: Iterate on arbitration weights based on observed fairness telemetry, enable webhook preemption hooks, expand to 10 tenants. Phase 3: General availability with docs, SDK examples, and billing attribution (no pricing change). Each phase requires SRE runbook updates and a rollback toggle in control plane.
monitoring_and_alerts: Dashboards with reservation success/preempt counts, preemption latency, autoscaler warmup failure rate. Alerts: reservation_success_rate < 80% for pilot tenants, preemption_webhook_failure_rate > 5%, unexpected increase in non-reserved tail latency > 25%
security_and_compliance: Reservation metadata stored in control plane; tenancy isolation policies apply. No customer data is included in reservation records. Ensure webhook URLs are validated and support signing of preemption events. Follow KMS key usage for audit logs as per Dedicated privacy controls.
dependencies: ENG-50122 (autoscaler: prewarm API and warmup signals)
ENG-51300 (control plane reservation state machine and datastore schema)
ENG-52011 (auditing pipeline: reservation events and traces)
open_questions: What should the default priority_tier be for free trial tenants?
Should we expose a reservation 'cost_estimate' in the response to help tenants decide fallback vs extend?
How aggressive should the autoscaler be for prewarming given multi-tenant risk (default cap recommended)?
Do we want to allow cross-tenant credit transfers in future iterations? (out of scope now)
implementation_notes: Backend will use a reservation index keyed by zone and pod-type. Arbitration will run as a deterministic comparator executed by the allocator service; decisions must be idempotent and safe to re-run. Preemption will prefer voluntary releases and will attempt a 5s webhook before force reclaim. The first iteration will not support transactional cross-zone atomicity.
